item.title: The Astronomy Book
item.description:
Timeline of discoveries

  • 2nd century BCE Aristarchus and one other astronomer believed in heliocentric model
  • 130 BCE : Hipparchus of Nicea noticed that star named Spica had moved 2 degrees east of the point of celestial sphere, called fall equinox point, compared to position recorded 150 years earlier. Then he found all stars position had shifted. This shift got known as “precession of the equinoxes”.
  • 15th century : Copernicus revives heliocentric model of solar system
  • 1748: Bradley discovered Nutation
  • 1814: A German maker of optical instruments named Joseph von Fraunhofer invented the spectroscope.
  • 1860: Kirchhoff showed that different patterns of dark lines are the spectral fingerprints of different chemical elements.
  • 1919: Rutherford transmuted atoms of N into O by firing particles at them from a radioactive element. That gave evidence to the fact that nuclear processes could produce new elements and release unimaginable quantities of energy.
  • 1979: Gravitational Lensing

Movement

  • A planet moves most rapidly when it is nearest the sun, at perihelion; a planet’s slowest motion occurs when it is farthest from the sun, at aphelion.
  • As an object’s velocity (v) approaches light speed (c), the object becomes increasingly squashed in the direction of travel when viewed by a stationary observer. This is not merely an illusion. In the observer’s frame of reference, the object’s shape really does change.
  • For example, the protons accelerated by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) particle accelerator travel very close to the speed of light—within 99.999 percent. Additional energy does very little to this speed, and instead boosts mass. At full power, the protons in the LHC are nearly 7,500 times more massive than they were when stationary.
  • Slipher said that spiral nebulae were separate galaxies outside The Milky Way. Hubble used this result to confirm that the universe was expanding.

Sun

  • If the sun became a black hole, its event horizon would be 2 miles (3 km) from the center. A black hole with Earth’s mass would have a 1⁄3-in (9-mm) radius.
  • Payne in 1925 showed some crazy findings about heilum and hydrogen levels in stars which Henry Russell thought were crazy. Four years after, he conceded that she was right. And this established that most stars are chemically similar. She found way to determine temperature of any star from its spectrum. And showed that hydrogen and helium are dominant elements in universe - key step towards Big Bang Theory.
  • Since all gases obey the same laws, assuming that the sun is not only gaseous at the surface but throughout allows the calculation of the temperature and pressure at the center.
  • Einstein’s insight led many to revisit the idea that the universe started small, among them the Belgian priest Georges Lemaître, whose 1931 proposal would carry echoes of The Rigveda.

Telescope

  • With naked eye, the resolution that we see of moon is around 1/30.
  • With lens of 1, 2, 4 cm diameter, the resolution improves to 1/120, 1/240, 1/480 degrees respectively.

Bodies

  • Asteroids are irregular in shape if they have D < 380 km ( Hughes-Cole Limit )

  • Comet nuclei are among the darkest objects in the solar system. Only 4 percent of the light that falls on them is reflected. Fresh black asphalt, by comparison, reflects nearly twice as much.

  • The object that causes the glowing trail is called a meteor. If any of it survives to reach the ground, it is termed a meteorite.

  • Gravitational weight of a taller mountain would exceed the strength of the underlying mantle rock in case of Earth, that’s why we don’t have mountains bigger than Everest like 8.8km. So, in planets with lower mass, weight of objects is less, so there can be bigger mountains. e.g. Mars Mount Olympus is 3x higher than Everest. Mass of Mars is about 1/10th and diameter about 1/2 of Earth.

  • Small wobble in precession with an 18.6 year cycle. Both precession and nutation are caused by gravitational interactions between moon, earth and the sun.

  • Stars that changed in brightness with a regular period. Discovered by Goodricke with Delta Cephei star in constellation of Cepheus.

    • Cepheid variables are reasonably easy to recognize because they are among the brightest variable stars, and they have a characteristic light curve, showing fairly rapid increases in brightness followed by a slower tailing off. Today, they are known to be giant yellow stars that “pulsate”—varying in diameter as well as brightness over their cycles—and are very rare.
    • Hertzsprung proposed that there was a definite relationship between periods and average intrinsic brightness. Then by comparing its intrinsic brightness to its apparent magnitude (measured average brightness from Earth), it should be possible to calculate the distance to the Cepheid variable.
    • Using statistical parallax, he tried to calculate distances to Cepheids in the Milky way galaxy.
    • 1923 : Hubble measured distance to Cepheid in the Andromeda galaxy leading to understanding that Andromeda nebula was a different galaxy.
    • The star RS Puppis is one of the brightest Cepheid variables in the Milky Way. It is about 6,500 light-years from Earth and has a cycle of variability lasting 41.4 days.
    • Today, classical Cepheids are used to measure the distance of galaxies out to about 100 million light-years—well beyond the local group of galaxies.
    • Classical Cepheids have also been used to clarify many characteristics of the Milky Way galaxy, such as its local spiral structure and the sun’s distance from the plane of the galaxy. Type II Cepheids have been used to measure distances to galactic center and globular clusters.
    • These stars expand and contract over a regular cycle, at the same time regularly varying in brightness. They are hottest and brightest shortly after reaching their most contracted phase. The graph of the star’s luminosity (light output) against time is called its light curve.

  • Many meteorites contain small particles called chondrules. Some of the oldest materials in solar system and can tell about meteorite’s early composition.

  • Orbital resonance occurs when the gravity of orbiting bodies produces a stable and self-correcting system. An example is the orbits of the neighboring giant planets Jupiter and Saturn, whose orbital periods are in a ratio of 5:2.

  • Parallax is the apparent movement of a nearby object against distant objects due to the changing position of the observer.

  • It was discovered that there are long periods in each cycle when the number of sunspots is low.

  • Edward Pickering employed a large team of women to carry out the work of classification of stars based on temperature sequence.

item.title: The Code Breaker
item.description:
Gene Editing Ethical Considerations

  • What happens to our societal structure when endowments that came via random lottery are no longer random? What will happen to our feelings of empathy and acceptance?

Jennifer Doudna

  • Family Diary of struggles
  • Study in 2019 of more than six million articles with women as the principal author showed that they are less likely to use self-promotional terms, such as “novel” and “unique” and “unprecedented,” to describe their findings.

CRISPR

  • The one Doudna and others developed in 2012 was based on a virus fighting trick used by bacteria, which have been battling viruses for more than a billion years. In their DNA, bacteria develop clustered repeated sequences known as CRISPRs.
  • DNA as repository of genetic information was made in 1944 by Oswald Avery and colleagues at Rockefeller University in New York. By extracting DNA from a strain of bacteria, mixing it with other, they showed that DNA transmitted inheritable transformations.
  • Innovation using cross-study has been very integral in Biology.
  • Bacterias in soil are able to communicate and join when they are starved for nutrients.
  • RNA was just seen as messenger molecule that carries instructiions from DNA that is nestled in the nucleus of cells. So, small segment of DNA that encodes a gene is transcribed into snippet of RNA, which then travels to manufacturing region of the cell. Then it facilitates the assembly of proper sequence of amino acids to make a specified protien.
  • Cech and Altman discovered that there were certain RNA introns that were self-splicing.
  • Doudna used many tactics to create an RNA enzyme, or ribozyme, that could stitch together little RNA pieces. She and Szostak engineered a ribozyme that could splice together a copy a itself.
  • Transposons or jumping genes which can change their position in a genome.
  • RNA is made up of very few chemicals, so it accomplishes complex tasks based on the different ways it is folded. One of the challenges with RNA is that it’s a molecule made of only four chemical building blocks, unlike proteins, which have twenty.
  • RNA interference: Normally the genes encoded by DNA in cells dispatch messenger RNAs to direct the building of a protein. RNA interference is when small molecules find a way to mess with these messenger RNAs. It operates by deploying an enzyme called “Dicer”. Dicer sinps a long piece of RNA into short fragments. Then these fragments do a search and destroy mission: seek out a messenger molecule that has matching letters, then they use a scissors-like enzyme to chop it up. Then that genetic information carried by that messenger RNA is silenced.
  • Later spanish scientist also discribed a different virus fighting mechanism that didn’t work with RNA interference, but much more interesting.
  • Ishino found that there were five identical segments of DNA in bacterias which usually have very less amount of DNA material to begin with. So, this had to be something important. These were “spacers”.
  • Mojica named it “Clustered regularly interspaced short pallindromic repeats”
  • When he searched for spacers in previous databases, he found that those segments matched sequences that were in viruses that attacked E. Coli. Other bacterias had this crispr sequence as well.
  • Bacterias were taking the virus’s DNA and acquired immunity to that new virus.
  • DNAs and protiens alike cannot be defined just by their sequence: you need to know how its folded in terms of its structure.
  • Enzymes are protiens that spark chemical reactions in the cells of living beings. There are 5000+ biochemical reactions catalyzed by enzymes. e.g. Breaking down starches and protiens, causing muscle contractions, regulating metabolism, and in this case: cutting and splicing DNA and RNA.
  • These CRISPR associated enzymes also known as Cas. enzymes enable the system to cut and paste new memories of viruses that attack that bacteria. They create short segments of RNA called CRISPR RNA (crRNA) that can guide a scissors-like enzyme to dangerous virus and cut up its genetic material.
  • By the time Gentech was hiring Doudna, the company already was worth 100 billion.
  • RNA hairpin where Cas6 could interact with just the right sequence.
  • Charpentier, on the other hand, was more nomadic. Since she felt more like foreigner, she found more delight in her work than anything else.
  • A gene known as P53 encodes for a protein that suppresses the growth of cancerous tumors. It helps the body respond to damaged DNA and prevents cancerous cells from dividing. Cancers proliferates if something goes wrong with this gene.
  • Elephants have 20 copies of this gene and rarely get cancer.
  • Zayner, biotechnology at home.
  • Then they found anti CRISPR cas9s that would inhibit or stop the editing. That made sure that process could be much more.
  • And with gene therapy there were incidents where people died due to immune response which made it more challenging to work with and continue progress.

Highlights

One of the leaders she tapped was a postdoc named Jennifer Hamilton who, a few months earlier, had spent a day teaching me to use CRISPR to edit human genes. I was pleased, but also a bit unnerved, to see how easy it was. Even I could do it!

item.title: Why we Sleep
item.description:
Consequences of not getting enough sleep

  • Routinely sleeping less than six or seven hours a night demolishes your immune system, more than doubling your risk of cancer. Insufficient sleep is a key lifestyle factor determining whether or not you will develop Alzheimer’s disease. Inadequate sleep—even moderate reductions for just one week—disrupts blood sugar levels so profoundly that you would be classified as pre-diabetic. Short sleeping increases the likelihood of your coronary arteries becoming blocked and brittle, setting you on a path toward cardiovascular disease, stroke, and congestive heart failure.
  • It is disquieting to learn that vehicular accidents caused by drowsy driving exceed those caused by alcohol and drugs combined.

Dream and Sleep in all organisms

  • Dreaming provides a unique suite of benefits to all species fortunate enough to experience it, humans included. Among these gifts are a consoling neuro-chemical bath that mollifies painful memories and a virtual reality space in which the brain melds past and present knowledge, inspiring creativity.
  • A balanced diet and exercise are of vital importance, yes. But we now see sleep as the preeminent force in this health trinity. The physical and mental impairments caused by one night of bad sleep dwarf those caused by an equivalent absence of food or exercise.
  • We have no scientific consensus as to why our sleep (and that of all other mammals and birds) cycles in this repeatable but dramatically asymmetric pattern, though a number of theories exist.
  • Without exception, every animal species studied to date sleeps, or engages in something remarkably like it. This includes insects, such as flies, bees, cockroaches, and scorpions;I fish, from small perch to the largest sharks;II amphibians, such as frogs; and reptiles, such as turtles, Komodo dragons, and chameleons.
  • How “old” does this make sleep? Worms emerged during the Cambrian explosion: at least 500 million years ago. That is, worms (and sleep by association) predate all vertebrate.
  • We have discovered that the very simplest forms of unicellular organisms that survive for periods exceeding twenty-four hours, such as bacteria, have active and passive phases that correspond to the light-dark cycle of our planet.
  • One evolutionary function that demands more sleep is the need to service an increasingly complex nervous system.
  • For now, our most accurate estimate of why different species need different sleep amounts involves a complex hybrid of factors, such as dietary type (omnivore, herbivore, carnivore), predator/prey balance within a habitat, the presence and nature of a social network, metabolic rate, and nervous system complexity.
  • Only birds and mammals, which appeared later in the evolutionary timeline of the animal kingdom, have full-blown REM sleep.
  • When a theme repeats in evolution, and independently across unrelated lineages, it often signals a fundamental need.
  • Take cetaceans, such as dolphins and whales, for example. Their sleep, of which there is only NREM, can be unihemispheric, meaning they will sleep with half a brain at a time! One half of the brain must always stay awake to maintain life-necessary movement in the aquatic environment.
  • Sleep with both sides of the brain, or sleep with just one side and then switch. Both are possible, but sleep you must. Sleep is non-negotiable.
  • Biphasic sleep is encoded in our genetic code.
  • The practice of natural biphasic sleep, and a healthy diet, appear to be the keys to a long-sustained life.
  • The sociocultural complexity and cognitive intelligence in humans could have been enhanced because of REM sleep, the act of dreaming itself.

Cicardian Rhythm

  • The first was that humans, like de Mairan’s heliotrope plants, generated their own endogenous circadian rhythm in the absence of external light from the sun.
  • The second unexpected—and more profound—result was that their reliably repeating cycles of wake and sleep were not precisely twenty-four hours in length, but consistently and undeniably longer than twenty-four hours.
  • We have now determined that the average duration of a human adult’s endogenous circadian clock runs around twenty-four hours and fifteen minutes in length.
  • Although the temperature drop helps to initiate sleep, the temperature change itself will rise and fall across the twenty-four-hour period regardless of whether you are awake or asleep.

More biology and its consequences

  • An adult’s owlness or larkness, also known as their chronotype, is strongly determined by genetics. If you are a night owl, it’s likely that one (or both) of your parents is a night owl.
  • Melatonin simply provides the official instruction to commence the event of sleep, but does not participate in the sleep race itself.
  • For every day you are in a different time zone, your suprachiasmatic nucleus can only readjust by about one hour.
  • You may have noticed that it feels harder to acclimate to a new time zone when traveling eastward than when flying westward.
  • Even sunlight coming through thick cloud on a rainy day is powerful enough to help reset our biological clocks.

What causes sleep and what can inhibit it

  • The longer you are awake, the more adenosine will accumulate. One consequence of increasing adenosine in the brain is an increasing desire to sleep.
  • By hijacking and occupying these receptors, caffeine blocks the sleepiness signal normally communicated to the brain by adenosine.
  • Caffeine has an average half-life of five to seven hours.
  • Across the night, sleep lifts the heavy weight of sleep pressure, lightening the adenosine load. After approximately eight hours of healthy sleep in an adult, the adenosine purge is complete.
  • First, after waking up in the morning, could you fall back asleep at ten or eleven a.m.? If the answer is “yes,” you are likely not getting sufficient sleep quantity and/or quality. Second, can you function optimally without caffeine before noon? If the answer is “no,” then you are most likely self-medicating your state of chronic sleep deprivation.

Phases of Sleep

  • Kleitman and Aserinsky further demonstrated that REM sleep, in which brain activity was almost identical to that when we are awake, was intimately connected to the experience we call dreaming, and is often described as dream sleep.
  • NREM sleep received further dissection in the years thereafter, being subdivided into four separate stages, unimaginatively named NREM stages 1 to 4 (we sleep researchers are a creative bunch), increasing in their depth.
  • Stages 3 and 4 are therefore the deepest stages of NREM sleep you experience, with “depth” being defined as the increasing difficulty required to wake an individual out of NREM stages 3 and 4, compared with NREM stages 1 or 2.
  • In the first half of the night, the vast majority of our ninety-minute cycles are consumed by deep NREM sleep, and very little REM sleep, as can be seen in cycle 1 of the figure above. But as we transition through into the second half of the night, this seesaw balance shifts, with most of the time dominated by REM sleep, with little, if any, deep NREM sleep.
  • A key function of deep NREM sleep, which predominates early in the night, is to do the work of weeding out and removing unnecessary neural connections. In contrast, the dreaming stage of REM sleep, which prevails later in the night, plays a role in strengthening those connections.
  • What you are actually experiencing during deep NREM sleep is one of the most epic displays of neural collaboration that we know of. Through an astonishing act of self-organization, many thousands of brain cells have all decided to unite and “sing,” or fire, in time.
  • For these reasons, REM sleep has also been called paradoxical sleep: a brain that appears awake, yet a body that is clearly asleep.
  • When it comes to information processing, think of the wake state principally as reception (experiencing and constantly learning the world around you), NREM sleep as reflection (storing and strengthening those raw ingredients of new facts and skills), and REM sleep as integration (interconnecting these raw ingredients with each other, with all past experiences, and, in doing so, building an ever more accurate model of how the world works, including innovative insights and problem-solving abilities).
  • The brain paralyzes the body so the mind can dream safely.

Correlation of human sleep with brain development

  • Autistic individuals show a 30 to 50 percent deficit in the amount of REM sleep they obtain, relative to children without autism.
  • The challenge for development was to build and add vast numbers of neural highways and interconnections that become a fledgling brain. As we have discussed, REM sleep plays an essential role in this proliferation process.
  • A second round of remodeling must take place. It does so during late childhood and adolescence. Here, the architectural goal is not to scale up, but to scale back for the goal of efficiency and effectiveness. The time of adding brain connections with the help of REM sleep is over. Instead, pruning of connections becomes the order of the day or, should I say, night. Enter the sculpting hand of deep NREM sleep.
  • Deep sleep may be a driving force of brain maturation, not the other way around.
  • Adolescents face two other harmful challenges in their struggle to obtain sufficient sleep as their brains continue to develop. The first is a change in their circadian rhythm. The second is early school start times.
  • Asking your teenage son or daughter to go to bed and fall asleep at ten p.m. is the circadian equivalent of asking you, their parent, to go to sleep at seven or eight p.m.
  • Furthermore, asking that same teenager to wake up at seven the next morning and function with intellect, grace, and good mood is the equivalent of asking you, their parent, to do the same at four or five a.m.
  • This ingenious biological solution selectively shifts teenagers to a later phase when they can, for several hours, operate independently.
  • That older adults simply need less sleep is a myth. Older adults appear to need just as much sleep as they do in midlife, but are simply less able to generate that (still necessary) sleep.

Sleep and its impact on humans

  • Elderly individuals fail to connect their deterioration in health with their deterioration in sleep, despite causal links between the two having been known to scientists for many decades.
  • Even when controlling for factors such as body mass index, gender, race, history of smoking, frequency of exercise, and medications, the lower an older individual’s sleep efficiency score, the higher their mortality risk, the worse their physical health, the more likely they are to suffer from depression, the less energy they report, and the lower their Cognitive Functions, typified by forgetfulness.
  • Add these things up, and a self-perpetuating cycle ensues wherein many seniors are battling a sleep Debt, trying to stay awake later in the evening, inadvertently dozing off earlier, finding it hard to fall or stay asleep at night, only to be woken up earlier than they wish because of a regressed circadian rhythm.
  • Those who were awake throughout the day became progressively worse at Learning, even though their ability to Concentration remained stable (determined by separate attention and response time tests). In contrast, those who napped did markedly better, and actually improved in their capacity to memorize facts.
  • Sleep six hours or less and you are shortchanging the brain of a learning restoration benefit that is normally performed by sleep spindles. That sleep sets in motion the process of memory consolidation was recognized long ago, and may be one of the oldest proposed functions of sleep.
  • Even daytime naps as short as twenty minutes can offer a Memory Consolidation advantage, so long as they contain enough NREM sleep.
  • Sleep is able to offer a far more discerning hand in memory improvement: one that preferentially picks and chooses what information is, and is not, ultimately strengthened.
  • Final benefit of sleep for memory is arguably the most remarkable of all: creativity. Sleep provides a nighttime theater in which your brain tests out and builds connections between vast stores of information.
  • Ten days of six hours of sleep a night was all it took to become as impaired in performance as going without sleep for twenty-four hours straight. When participants were asked about their subjective sense of how impaired they were, they consistently underestimated their degree of performance disability. Its like they can’t even know that they are under-performing. After being awake for nineteen hours, people who were sleep-deprived were as cognitively impaired as those who were legally drunk. The recycle rate of a human being is around sixteen hours. After sixteen hours of being awake, the brain begins to fail.
  • Power naps may momentarily increase basic concentration under conditions of sleep deprivation, as can caffeine up to a certain dose. But in the subsequent studies that Dinges and many other researchers (myself included) have performed, neither naps nor caffeine can salvage more complex functions of the brain, including learning, memory, emotional stability, complex reasoning, or decision-making.
  • “The number of people who can survive on five hours of sleep or less without any impairment, expressed as a percent of the population, and rounded to a whole number, is zero.”
  • A structure located in the left and right sides of the brain, called the amygdala—a key hot spot for triggering strong emotions such as anger and rage, and linked to the fight-or-flight response—showed well over a 60 percent amplification in emotional reactivity in the participants who were sleep-deprived. You basically start getting irritated because of sleep deprivation.
  • The two most feared diseases throughout developed nations are dementia and Cancer. Both are related to inadequate sleep.
  • A lack of sleep is fast becoming recognized as a key lifestyle factor determining whether or not you will develop Alzheimer’s disease.
  • Without sufficient sleep, amyloid plaques build up in the brain, especially in deep-sleep-generating regions, attacking and degrading them.
  • Adults forty-five years or older who sleep fewer than six hours a night are 200 percent more likely to have a Heart Attack or stroke during their lifetime, as compared with those sleeping seven to eight hours a night.
  • In the first of these studies, participants were limited to sleeping four hours a night for just six nights. By the end of that week, these (formerly healthy) participants were 40 percent less effective at absorbing a standard dose of glucose, compared to when they were fully rested.
  • Inadequate sleep is the perfect recipe for obesity: greater calorie intake, lower calorie expenditure.
  • Van Cauter noticed that cravings for sweets (e.g., cookies, chocolate, and ice cream), heavy-hitting carbohydrate-rich foods (e.g., bread and pasta), and salty snacks (e.g., potato chips and pretzels) all increased by 30 to 40 percent when sleep was reduced by several hours each night. You become like a zombie craving without even knowing why.
  • Short sleep (of the type that many adults in first-world countries commonly and routinely report) will increase hunger and appetite, compromise impulse control within the brain, increase food consumption (especially of high-calorie foods), decrease feelings of food satisfaction after eating, and prevent effective weight loss when dieting.
  • Sleep fights against infection and sickness by deploying all manner of weaponry within your immune arsenal, cladding you with protection. When you do fall ill, the immune system actively stimulates the sleep system, demanding more bed rest to help reinforce the war effort.
  • A large European study of almost 25,000 individuals demonstrated that sleeping six hours or less was associated with a 40 percent increased risk of developing cancer, relative to those sleeping seven hours a night or more.
  • Michael Corke died of a rare, genetically inherited disorder called fatal familial insomnia (FFI). There are no treatments for this disorder, and there are no cures. Every patient diagnosed with the disorder has died within ten months, some sooner. It is one of the most mysterious conditions in the annals of medicine, and it has taught us a shocking lesson: a lack of sleep will kill a human being.
  • In other words, sleep may have more of an influence on Exercise than exercise has on sleep. It is still a clear bidirectional relationship, however, with a significant trend toward increasingly better sleep with increasing levels of physical activity, and a strong influence of sleep on daytime physical activity.
  • One brief note of caution regarding physical activity: try not to exercise right before bed. Body temperature can remain high for an hour or two after physical exertion. Should this occur too close to bedtime, it can be difficult to drop your core temperature sufficiently to initiate sleep due to the exercise-driven increase in metabolic rate.
  • Best to get your workout in at least two to three hours before turning the bedside light out (none LED-powered, I trust).
  • For healthy sleep, the scientific evidence suggests that you should avoid going to bed too full or too hungry, and shy away from diets that are excessively biased toward carbohydrates (greater than 70 percent of all energy intake), especially sugar.
  • Sleep appears to be a natural analgesic, and without it, pain is perceived more acutely by the brain, and, most importantly, felt more powerfully by the individual.

Importance of dreams in general

  • The scientists were able to predict with significant accuracy the content of participants’ dreams at any one moment in time using just the MRI scans, operating completely blind to the dream reports of the participants. Using the template data from the MRI images, they could tell if you were dreaming of a man or a woman, a dog or a bed, flowers or a knife. They were, in effect, mind reading, or should I say, dream reading.

  • This was the theory of overnight therapy. It postulated that the process of REM-sleep dreaming accomplishes two critical goals: (1) sleeping to remember the details of those valuable, salient experiences, integrating them with existing knowledge and putting them into autobiographical perspective, yet (2) sleeping to forget, or dissolve, the visceral, painful emotional charge that had previously been wrapped around those memories.

  • Cartwright had shown that it was not enough to have REM sleep, or even generic dreaming, when it comes to resolving our emotional past. Her patients required REM sleep with dreaming, but dreaming of a very specific kind: that which expressly involved dreaming about the emotional themes and sentiments of the waking trauma.

  • Upon awakenings from NREM sleep, participants did not appear to be especially creative, solving few of the anagram puzzles. But it was a different story when I woke them up out of REM sleep, from the dreaming phase. Overall, problem-solving abilities rocketed up, with participants solving 15 to 35 percent more puzzles when emerging from REM sleep compared with awakenings from NREM sleep or during daytime waking performance!

  • Overall, problem-solving abilities rocketed up, with participants solving 15 to 35 percent more puzzles when emerging from REM sleep compared with awakenings from NREM sleep or during daytime waking performance! Solutions seemed more effortless when the brain was being bathed by the afterglow of dream sleep.

  • When awake, we see only a narrow set of all possible memory interrelationships. The opposite is true, however, when we enter the dream state and start looking through the other (correct) end of the memory-surveying telescope. Using that wide-angle dream lens, we can apprehend the full constellation of stored information and their diverse combinatorial possibilities, all in creative servitude.

  • REM sleep is capable of creating abstract overarching knowledge and super-ordinate concepts out of sets of information.

  • REM sleep is especially dominant during this early-life window, and it is that REM sleep that plays a critical role in the development of language, we believe.

  • Scientists had gained objective, brain-based proof that lucid dreamers can control when and what they dream while they are dreaming.

item.title: The Beginning of Infinity
item.description:
Author: David Deutsch

Completed on: 2025-01-04

Summary

Good Explanations

  • Deutsch attributes all progress, both theoretical and practical, to quest for good explanations.
  • Good explanations go far beyond extrapolations from experience of the creators.
  • Unique thing about humans is the ability to create good explanations. Everyrhing we do to improve our lives attributes to this ability.
  • The real source of our theories is conjecture, and the real source of our knowledge is conjecture alternating with criticism. We create theories by rearranging, combining,altering and adding to existing ideas with the intention of improving upon them. The role of experiment and observation is to choose between existing theories, not to be the source of new ones.
    • In fact this is the main thing about innovation in general: there is no rational definition of where to look for answers or good questions. And there is no bad theory as long as our main basis for it is criticism with proper logic.
  • They even go beyond biological knowledge which has limited reach. Another difference is that mutations are random; conjectures are intentional.
  • We have known the world both to be more bigger and violent, but also awesome in detail. And the more we get good explanations, the elegance increases as well.
  • Good explanations make it harder to even fool yourselves. Its hard to vary it specifically for cases it doesn’t work with. And since it has an autonomous meaning and autonomous domain of applicability.
    • e.g. It might touch in places where you don’t even want it to touch and if its a good explanation, it will work there effectively as well.
    • That’s what is up with autonomic nature of it.
  • Old ways of thought, which did not seek good explanations, permitted no process such as science for correcting errors and misconceptions. Improvements happened so rarely that most people never experienced one. Ideas were static for long periods. Being bad explanations, even the best of them typically had little reach and were therefore brittle and unreliable beyond, and often within, their traditional applications.
  • We need to understand the contradictory ideas together in one piece: we will never run out of problems but we will keep creating good explanations and improve on our ability to do so at an exponential pace too.

Philosophical Ideas and Contrasts

  • Empiricism was the first basis from where our experimental science as we know today started.
  • We haven’t experienced Big Bang or billion light years; yet we have good explanations of it. With Inductivism ,we couldn’t have even understood about the stars and the universe except the fact that they are just dots.
  • Then comes the idea of Fallibilism
  • One good question he asks is why did our ancestors not have the same understanding we had although they had same brains and eyes like us anatomically. Its not for their lack of trying, nor for their lack of thinking. But they never could understand what’s beneath that appearance. He attributes it to this: They wanted to create knowledge, in order to make progress, but they did not know how.
  • This is why the Royal Society (one of the earliest scientific academies, founded in London in 1660) took as its motto ‘Nullius in verba’, which means something like ‘Take no one’s word for it’.

  • Its hard to predict human future and that must be understood as that and that alone.
  • There is a saying that an ounce of prevention equals a pound of cure. But that is only when one knows what to prevent. No precautions can avoid problems that we do not yet foresee. To prepare for those, there is nothing we can do but increase our ability to put things right if they go wrong. Trying to rely on the sheer good luck of avoiding bad outcomes indefinitely would simply guarantee that we would eventually fail without the means of recovering.
  • Only an open ended journey of creation and exploration will save us from what lies ahead. That is the only sustainable source of safety for us.

Infinity

  • But only a starting point of an infinite adventure. All you need do is make the decision [to end your static society]. It is yours to make.’ [With that decision] came the end, the final end of Eternity. – And the beginning of Infinity. – Isaac Asimov, The End of Eternity (1955)
  • Earth is smaller in terms of the space that we understand now.
  • What we know is still nowhere near what we can know. Yet, time and again, people think the knowledge that they possess is fairly close to the limit of what is knowable. Even Feynman thought that we were at crux and already towards the closed end of what can be discovered and known.
  • Future is not yet imaginable, so very exciting in that regards.
  • Even just from 1894, we know about space time, electromagnetism, cosmology, computation and so on. Even the people who thought that their generations had discovered the crux of it led to more discoveries in the future. A future they could never even have imagined.
  • If people thought of it like that, perhaps no one would need to be reminded that science claims neither infallibility nor finality. Such an important thing.
  • So, knowledge is going from problems to better problems.
  • Prophetic fallcy has always been strong even in the community that appreciates scientific attitude.
  • Infinite ignorance is a necessary condition for there to be infinite potential for knowledge.
  • The quest for good explanations is “open ended, and infinite”.
  • No need to choose nihilism over ambiguity as an answer. Scientific attitude doesn’t need to mean 100% truth. It needs to be understood as quest for good explanations.
  • We are not denying that some problems are fundamental and we are not able to create good explanations for that. It doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be working on them, or we have saturated in our ability to create good explanations.
  • One aspect is the ancient tension between the discrete and the continuous. Just like the tension between quantum theory and general theory of relativity.
  • Is there a bound on the number of computational steps that a computer can execute during the lifetime of the universe? If there is, then physics will also impose a bound on the amount of knowledge that can be created – knowledge-creation being a form of computation.
  • Everyone’s first thought was that unbounded knowledge-creation is possible only in a universe that does not recollapse. However, on analysis it turned out that the reverse is true: in universes that expand for ever, the inhabitants would run out of energy. But the cosmologist Frank Tipler discovered that in certain types of recollapsing universes the Big Crunch singularity is suitable for performing the faster-and-faster trick that we used in Infinity Hotel: an infinite sequence of computational steps could be executed in a finite time before the singularity, powered by the ever-increasing tidal effects of the gravitational collapse itself.
  • So, when we talk about infinities, there are infinite ways to harness time and energy in such events. To the inhabitants – who would eventually have to upload their personalities into computers made of something like pure tides – the universe would last for ever because they would be thinking faster and faster, without limit, as it collapsed, and storing their memories in ever smaller volumes so that access times could also be reduced without limit. Tipler called such universes ‘omega-point universes’. At the time, the observational evidence was consistent with the real universe being of that type.
  • A small part of the revolution that is currently overtaking cosmology is that the omega-point models have been ruled out by observation. Evidence – including a remarkable series of studies of supernovae in distant galaxies – has forced cosmologists to the unexpected conclusion that the universe not only will expand for ever but has been expanding at an accelerating rate. Something has been counteracting its gravity.
  • We do not know what. Pending the discovery of a good explanation, the unknown cause has been named ‘dark energy’. Depending on what dark energy turns out to be, it may well be possible to harness it in the distant future, to provide energy for knowledge-creation to continue for ever.
  • There are many different explanations of the bounded or unbounded nature of knowledge creation based on what we understand from Physics.
  • Because the Big Bang happened a finite time ago, and because of the finiteness of the speed of light, we shall only ever see a finite portion of infinite space – but that portion will continue to grow for ever.
  • Light becomes fainter as it spreads out: there are fewer photons per unit area. That means that ever larger telescopes are needed to detect a given object at ever larger distances. So there may be a limit to how distant – and therefore how unlikely – a phenomenon we shall ever be able to see. Except, that is, for one type of phenomenon: a beginning of infinity. Specifically, any civilization that is colonizing the universe in an unbounded way will eventually reach our location.
  • We should really understand all our predictions as implicitly including the proviso ‘unless the creation of new knowledge intervenes’.
  • To attempt to predict anything beyond the relevant horizon is futile – it is prophecy – but wondering what is beyond it is not.
  • When wondering leads to conjecture, that constitutes speculation, which is not irrational either. In fact it is vital.
  • For instance, we know from universality that AI is attainable by writing computer programs, but we have no idea how to write (or evolve) the right one.
  • What is the difference between laws that are instantiated in physical reality and those that are not?
  • What is the difference between a computer simulation of a person (which must be a person, because of universality) and a recording of that simulation (which cannot be a person)? When there are two identical simulations under way, are there two sets of qualia or one? Double the moral value or not?
  • The world remains as mysterious to us as it was to Eratosthenes though the amount of good explanations might have increased 1000 folds.
  • The world is explicable. We don’t live in a senseless world.
  • There are higher levels of emergence and higher levels of explanation. Profound abstractions in mathematics, morality and aesthetics are accessible to us. Ideas of tremendous reach are possible. But there is also plenty in the world that does not and will not make sense until we ourselves work out how to rectify it. Death does not make sense. Stagnation does not make sense. A bubble of sense within endless senselessness does not make sense. Whether the world ultimately does make sense will depend on how people – the likes of us – chose to think and to act.
  • Many people have an aversion to infinity of various kinds. But there are some things that we do not have a choice about. There is only one way of thinking that is capable of making progress, or of surviving in the long run, and that is the way of seeking good explanations through creativity and criticism. What lies ahead of us is in any case infinity. All we can choose is whether it is an infinity of ignorance or of knowledge, wrong or right, death or life.
  • The better we come to understand phenomena remote from our everyday experience, the longer those chains of interpretation become, and every additional link necessitates more theory.

Behind it all is surely an idea so simple, so beautiful, that when we grasp it – in a decade, a century, or a millennium – we will all say to each other, how could it have been otherwise? John Archibald Wheeler, Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 480 (1986

item.title: 30 second brain
item.description:
• Human Brain is a fascinating topic and this book covers basics on human brain using very small concepts.
  • Each neuron will have at most one axon. Axons typically split into separate branches before connecting with dendrites of other neurons.
  • Grey matter: Called grey because of lack of myelination that makes other parts of brain seem white.
  • Hippocampus: Formation and Consolidation of Memories, Spatial Navigation.
  • Myelin coating: Insulates the axon from other nearby axons and dramatically increase the speed of nerve impulse / spikes traveling along.
  • Parietal Cortex: Experience of space and position and heavily involved in attentional processes.
  • Purkinje Cells:
    • Found excessively in cerebellum
    • One of the largest neurons in the brain
    • Elaborately branching dendritic structures.
    • Long-range inhibitory control over output parts of cerebellum, enabling fine motor co-ordination and error correction.
  • Brain Impulse:
    • 0.1 Volt
    • Lasts one- to two-thousandths of a second
    • Runs along axons at up to 480 kph (300 mph).
    • When meets synapse, triggers release of neurotransmitters.
  • Glial Cells:
    • 50 times more in number than neurons.
    • Help neurons wire together in developing brains
    • Help nurture neurons in adult brain
    • Insulate axons
    • Mop up dead cells
    • Recycle used neurotransmitters
    • Protect brain from infection
  • Neurotransmitters:
    • Small molecules to Medium Compounds to Giant Molecules : Peptides.
    • Stored in tiny spheres called synaptic vesicles.
    • Impulse releases them into synaptic gaps.
    • Many don’t trigger fast excitation or inhibition, but initiate quite slow metabolic processes in neurons, causing lasting changes in the strength of synaptic connections.
    • Can turn ON and OFF of important genes.
    • Nitric Oxide(NO) , a poisonous gas, is a most unlikely transmitter.
      • Cannot be stored in vesicles.
      • Released as it is produced within specialized active neurons.
      • Spreads into envelopes of brain, where it can affect many receptive neurons without the transmitting neuron having to be directly connected to them. Non-synaptic Signaling.
  • As needs change, different genes are turned on or off. This changing pattern of active genes is particularly notable in functioning of synapses.
  • Signals are dispatched from synapses to their central nuclei and there the DNA is ordered to turn on the required genes.
  • While genes certainly affect brain function, the fact that they can be influenced by the environment frees our behavior from rigid genetic determinism.
  • Cajal realized that Golgi’s images showed nervous system as a network of discrete cellular components. This allowed neurons to be studied as functional units of brain.
  • Brain Stem is the metencephalon, thalamus is diencephalon, and outer cortex is telencephalon.
  • Cerebellum:
    • Densely packed with cells
    • 10% of brain volume
    • Contains half the neurons found in entire central nervous system.
    • FUN FACT: We are unable to tickle ourselves due to cerebellum.
    • Forward Models : Predictions about sensory consequences of actions and cancel them out.
    • Inverse Models : Calculating movements necessary to achieve a desired action.
  • Brain Development:
    • Hollow tube formed from the skin of very early embryo.
    • Cells multiply more rapidly at the front of the tube, which enlarges, becoming the embryonic brain.
    • Newly produced cells transform into immature neurons.
    • By the time embryo is about 4 weeks old, they migrate to their destination, growing dendrites and axons and forming the first of what will be trillions of synaptic connections.
    • About half the embryonic connections are killed off. The ones that survive get myelinated.
    • Grey matter voluem increases gradually through childhood, peaks in early adolescence and shrinks as an adolescent becomes an adult.
    • Genomes don’t have all the recipe to make brain on their own: need to exploit information from the environment which helps fine tune the neuronal networks.
  • Different Animal Brains:
    • Fruit Fly Lacks cortex but has large antennal lobes and mushroom bodies dedicated to processing smell.
    • Rat has large areas of cortex devoted to processing information from its whiskers.
    • Fish has enlarged cerebellum for movement.
  • Humans are believed to have massive expansion of their brain due to bipedalism, larger social groups and the emergence of language.
  • Classic Conditioning:
    • Environment Stimulus.
    • Associated with a outcome.
    • Leads to new behavior with respect to the stimulus.
  • Instrumental Conditioning:
    • Association between action and outcome leading to increased propensity to do the action.
  • Connectionism:
    • Theoretical approach that emphasizes how interconnected network of nerusn can learn via simple local rules applied between pair of neurons.
  • Hypersynchronous state: Levels of neuronal synchrony exceed normal limits, so that large parts of brain start switching on and off together.
  • Phrenology: Individual variation in mental capabilities and personality characteristics can be inferred on the basis of differences in the shape of the skull.
  • Predictive Coding: Hermann von Helmholtz.
    • Perception as a form of inference.
  • Re-entrant connectivity : Neural signals flow in both direction between two areas.
  • Cognitive functions are neither fully localized nor wholly distributed in the brain.
  • Brain doesn’t have one language but many. Even worse, there may be a different language at different level: Neuronal, Ensemble and the whole brain.
  • Rate code vs Timing Code: How do distant groups of neurons co-ordinate their activity?
  • Alpha Waves: Hans Berger, inventor of EEG in 1920s.
    • Slow oscillations at about 10 Hz.
    • Predominantly across the back of the brain and more pronounced during relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed.
  • Delta Waves: 1-4 Hz.
  • Theta Waves: 4-8 Hz.
  • Beta Waves: 12 - 25 Hz
  • Gamma Waves: 25 - 70 Hz and higher.
  • These are not well established categories though.
  • Epileptic Seizures: When neural oscillations get too strong, the brain can enter a state of hypersynchrony similar to brainstorm.
  • Proposals of Theory of Neuronal Group Selection:
    • Early brain development generates a highly diverse population of neuronal circuits.
    • There is a selection among these groups. Those which are used survive and strengthen.
    • Re-entry: Constant interchange of signals between widely separated neuronal populations.
  • Helmholtz and Perception:
    • What’s out there? question must involve brain inferring the external causes of its sensory signals. This means brain something similar to Bayesian Inference that describes how beliefs are updated as new evidence comes in.
    • The incoming sensory data is combined with ‘prior beliefs’ to determine the best probable cause, which correspond to perception.
    • Then these prediction errors are used to update prior beliefs.
  • Double Mode Network:
    • Group of brain region whose activity is reduced during the performance of externally directed task, and is more active in states of wakeful rest, mind-wandering, introspection or inwardly directed attention.
    • Includes medial parts of prefrontal and temporal lobes and posterior cingulate cortex.
  • Diffusion Tensor Imaging:
    • Depends on the fact that water molecules diffuse preferentially along axons, instead of across them.
  • Electroencephalography:
    • Detecting tiny variations in electric field at the surface of the brain, which are produced by the activity of population of neurons in the underlying cortex.
  • fMRI extends MRI to measure brain activity and is based on measuring the differences in blood oxygenation that go along with neural activity. Good spatial resolution but poor time resolution compared to EEG.
  • Some believe that revealing the network structure of the human brain might yield fewer clues than promised. One species with complete connectome maped is Nematode worm, Caenorhabditis elegans. Yet it’s behavioral features remain a mystery.
  • Scientists have used virus to smuggle an algal light-sensitive gene into rat neurons. When exposed to blue light, the neurons fired. Soon an ‘off’ as well as ‘on’ switch was found.
  • Wim Vanduffel et. al modified a region of frontal lobes in two monkeys to enable widespread light-induced activation. With blue light turning this region on, the monkeys were faster at object-tracking task. Optogenetics thus acts a great promise.
  • Montreal Method : Operate on patients to excise the parts of the brain from which epileptic seizures originate. Under local anaesthetic and asked questions to patients what kind of sensations they have when probing different parts of the brain. The ‘homunculus’ produced with colleague Herbert Jasper, is still in use today.
  • Without a task to perform, brain is almost as active as normal, but a default set of regions lights up instead of task related ones.
  • Default mode network : Importance of this network comes from it’s most promising putative role, that is daydreaming, which has been linked to both higher insight and creativity.
  • Hemispheres of Brain:
    • Characterizing left hemisphere as cold, logical and right as emotional and creative is an over-simplification.
    • Instead of tasks being delegated to one side or the another, both typically apply a different processing style to the same tasks. Left hemisphere is dominant for language, while the right has language functions such as recognizing intonation.
  • On experimenting with electrical probe to simulate neurons, it was discovered that simulation of a single neuron in the temporal lobes would reactivate entire memories in the patient.
  • TMS : Non-invasive procedure in which a brief magnetic pulse on the scalp simulates underlying cortical region.
  • Autoscopic experience: Experience of seeing one’s body from an external perspective.
  • Comatose state: Patients in such state show no signs of wakefulness or awareness. The brain activity during such states is similar to that observed during general anaesthesia.
  • Prefrontal Parietal Network: Frequently associated with consciousness, especially in so-called global workspace theories.
  • Qualia : Philosophical term broadly referring to the intrinsic properties of conscious experience.
  • Causality of EEG Signals : A slowly rising electrical brain signal seems to precede voluntary decisions to perform actions.
  • Supplementary Motor Area : Part of the frontal lobes and a possible neural source of the readiness potential. Direct simulation of this region produces the experiences of wanting to make a movement.
  • Daniel Dennett : Consciousness in terms of function that it supports and not by the raw essence of experience.
  • Binocular Rivalry : One image [ e.g. house ] shown to one eye and another image [ face ] shown to another eye. Brain cannot resolve this ambiguous input into single image, one’s conscious experience alternates betwen the house and the face.
  • Phantom Limb Syndrome : Brain builds a body model that doesn’t always match the physical body.
  • Global Workspace Theory : Specific mental contents such as perceptions, thoughts, intentions to act etc. remain unconscious unless or until they gain access to a global workspace, which broadcasts their contents across the brain, making them available for the flexible control of behavior.
  • Thalamic switch Theory : GAs turn consciousness off by reducing activity in specific parts of thalamus.
  • V4 : Samir Zeki in 1970s and has been closely associated with perception of color, although not limited to it.
  • Change Blindness : A phenomenon in which surprisingly large changes in visual scene go unnoticed if there is a gap between the images of if there are other more salient changes accompanying the transition.
    • A bed of roses will result in different mixture of wavelength during the dawn and the day but we will perceive the roses as a particular shade of red in both cases.
  • Super Colliculus : A pair of small structures beneath the cerebral cortex that play an important role in guiding fast visual reflexes, such as object tracking.
  • Some of the colors (such as magenta) don’t have corresponding wavelength - brain constructs it.
  • The key to understanding this comes from the fact that there is not just one route that connects the eyes to the brain but many ( around 10 in humans ), so damaging the brain might affect one route selectively.
    • Routes have evolved for different functions- one uses light to calibrate the biological clock and another is used to orient the eyes to sudden changes.
    • Fast seeing route ( via super colliculus ) that moves the eyes and a slow seeing route ( via the cortex ) that can detect the details of what is seen.
  • Synaesthesia : For small % of population, words may be colored, music may have a taste, or numbers may be visualized on a twisting, turning landscape.
  • Attention Mechanism: Since vision and rest of our senses are continually bombarded with information, brain has developed this mechanism to filter and prioritize ( such as amplifying its neural signal ) at the expense of other information.
  • Object Tracking:
    • Need to know the position of eyes in the socket.
    • Need to know position of the head relative to the body.
    • Signals from eye and neck muscles need to be linked to vision.
    • There appears to be separate pathways in the brain for locating and acting on an object versus knowing what the object is.
  • Sacks : The Man who mistook his wife for a hat, 24 essays reporting in from the extremes of the mind.
  • Alien movements : If our motor cortex becomes disconnected from the controlling regions, then movements are produced that are unexpected.
  • Medial Temporal Lobes : Related to long term memories.
  • Fragmentation of storage areas:
    • Semantic Memories [ Capital of France is] : Temporal Lobe
    • Memories from past events: Widely distributed across temporal cortex.
  • Broca’s area : Inferior Frontal Gyrus, is thought to play a central role in processing syntax, grammar and sentence structure.
  • Wernicke’s area: Superior Temporal Gyrus : Involved in comprehension of language.
  • Metacognition:
    • Think about thinking.
    • Not only important for monitoring how we learn new information, but also for communicating our subjective experiences with others.
    • Macaque monkeys, Dolphins and rats exhibit signs of metacognition when performing a perceptual or memory task. Others, such as pigeons don’t.
  • Negative emotional impact is twice as intense as the positive effect of gains, which affects our decision making in predictable ways.
  • Mirror Neurons : Activated during the execution of an action and by the sight of someone else performing that action.
  • Pheromones : Airborne chemical signals released by male mice that stimulate neurogenesis in the olfactory bulb and hippocampus in the brain of female mice.
  • Volume of Posterior Superior Temporal Sulcus pSTS predicted the level of loneliness in sample of people. It is linked to the processing of social cues.
  • Splitting the brain in half proved to alleviate the symptoms of epilepsy without apparent impairment.
  • Thought Insertions : Patients experiencing a lack of ownership of their own thoughts.
  • Schizophrenia : Perceptual hallucinations, false beliefs, thought insertions. Symptoms may arise from a failure to properly combine prior expectations with new sensory evidence.
    • Genes related to it : COMT, is involved in breaking down the neurotransmitter dopamine, involved in prediction-based learning.
  • Four meditation sessions were sufficient to increase working memory capacity. Five sessions showed increased performance on an attentional task that involved resolving conflict. Lessen sense of anxiety, anger and tiredness.
